repos.title: StartLux-Decision: AutoThink Decision Models with Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Deliberative Decisions
repos.paper_summary: StartLux-Decision is a family of 0.8B–27B decision models that output probability distributions over candidate options for typed questions. The Instant variant makes one forward pass with bidirectional attention in its full-attention layers. The AutoThink variant first makes a one-pass prediction, then generates a reasoning trace of up to 4,096 tokens only when its top probability is below 0.9, and averages the initial and post-reasoning distributions. The final training stage adds reasoning supervision and RLCD2, which uses a frozen reference model, proper-score rewards, and a soft length penalty. RLCD2 raises the share of traces that finish within the generation limit by up to 48 percentage points and cuts average reasoning length by up to 65%, with accuracy largely preserved. On the public Decision Index 0.3 subset, Instant models beat the strongest comparable-scale open-weight decision models by 7.4–16.9 points, and the 27B AutoThink reaches 73.4. On DecisionPivot, a programmatically generated benchmark of contrast pairs, AutoThink beats its Instant counterpart by 11.5–18.4 points in pair accuracy. Policy-aware calibration reduces confidence–accuracy gaps to within 2.7 points across 184 settings. Stated limitations include generalization beyond represented task families and reliability under distribution shift, both left to future work.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Decision models need reasoning on hard cases without losing single-pass efficiency; the paper proposes two variants, RLCD2 training, and DecisionPivot.

digest_headlines.heading: Model Design and Training
digest_headlines.headline: Three-stage training gives Instant bidirectional attention and teaches AutoThink to reason only when its confidence is below 0.9.

digest_headlines.heading: RLCD2: Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Deliberative Decisions
digest_headlines.headline: RLCD2 rewards reasoning by the change in proper score and penalizes traces beyond a soft budget.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: On the public Decision Index 0.3 subset, Instant models lead comparable-scale references by 7.4–16.9 points.

digest_headlines.heading: Capability and Reliability Analysis
digest_headlines.headline: Selecting among candidates makes reported confidence overconfident, and policy-aware calibration narrows the gaps across 184 settings.

digest_headlines.heading: Efficient Inference and Deployment
digest_headlines.headline: Single-pass Instant readouts on a single GPU take 24–52 ms for 256-token prompts and 31–98 ms for 1,024-token prompts.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Future work targets generalization beyond represented task families and reliability under distribution shift.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix documents training data sources and decontamination, policy-aware calibration proofs, and serving configuration safeguards.

repos.title: LongBanana: An Expert-Verified Benchmark for Long-Context Multi-Reference Image Synthesis
repos.paper_summary: LongBanana is a benchmark of 90 expert-designed, expert-verified tasks for synthesizing one image from many reference images, with 4,670 atomic checklist items. Tasks average about 32 references and include hard-negative references that must be excluded. Each task is converted into an entity–relation graph, and items are scored on Content Fidelity, Relational Binding, and Global Constraint Satisfaction by LongBananaEval, an agentic judge that calls tools such as OCR and counting. Reviewers labeled 46,700 item judgments; a 15% double-labeled subset reached 89.4% exact agreement and 0.83 quadratic weighted kappa. On output-level Overall scores, LongBananaEval reaches Pearson 0.8707, versus 0.8413 for a single-pass VLM judge. For generation, the paper compares direct prompting, agent harnesses, and RPR workflows, with Nano Banana 2 as the image generator. The best system, OpenClaw + RPR, scores 78.4 average and 47.8 P@70%, against 74.6 and 35.6 for PD-Direct, a baseline given the construction graph. RPR gains depend on the harness, and the paper notes it can introduce drift.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Multi-reference image generation errors are provenance failures that holistic realism scores cannot localize.

digest_headlines.heading: The LongBanana Benchmark
digest_headlines.headline: LongBanana contains 90 cases across a 3-by-3 taxonomy, each scored through atomic graph-derived checklist items.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Nano Banana 2 under OpenClaw with RPR scores 78.4 overall, above the 68.4 of full-prompt direct generation.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Agentic workflows reach broader success than a fixed privileged schedule, and checklist scores localize failures.

digest_headlines.heading: Acknowledgments and Disclosure of Funding
digest_headlines.headline: Funding comes from two Guangdong programs and KlingAI Research, and the authors declare no other competing interests.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers related work, benchmark construction details, scorer and label quality statistics, extra experiments, and release safeguards.

repos.title: Fewer Tokens, Better Action: GPT-6 Astra Robot Agents with 14% Higher Success Rate but 65% Fewer Tokens
repos.paper_summary:
PyRUA-Lean is an interactive code-execution framework for vision-language model (VLM) robot agents that reduces token overhead while improving task success. The agent generates Python cells that compose classical robot primitives and learned vision-language-action policies, executing conditional checks and local retries within the runtime. Only explicitly requested images and state feedback are returned to the VLM for replanning, whereas intermediate results remain in a persistent program state.

Across 700 simulated task instances from LIBERO-PRO, RoboTwin 2.0, and RoboCasa365, PyRUA-Lean increases overall success from 63.1% to 71.7% compared to a tool-calling baseline using the same GPT-6 Astra planner. On instances solved by both agents, it uses 49% fewer LLM calls and 65% fewer input tokens, reducing estimated cost per episode from USD 1.63 to USD 0.74. Ablations show these gains persist without VLA policies or operating guides. Limitations include evaluation restricted to simulation with one run per instance, and efficiency gains diminish on tasks dominated by VLA policies where initial prompts account for much of the input cost.

repos.title: RoboScope Kit: Unified Interfaces for Fast and Scalable Embodied-AI Evaluation
repos.paper_summary: RoboScope Kit is a shared evaluation layer for robot-policy benchmarks. Each model is wrapped once as a Policy class, and each benchmark is wrapped once as an adapter around its native evaluator, so benchmark rules and scoring stay unchanged. A scheduler runs simulator workers and Policy replicas as separate pools, sizes both with a time-bounded concurrency search over short probes, and shards work deterministically across GPU instances. Runtime optimization renders only the observations a chunked Policy reads. Adapters cover six benchmark families. On LIBERO-Long with a StarVLA checkpoint on one RTX 4090, the search selects twelve workers and three replicas, which evaluate 500 episodes 4.45× faster than the official StarVLA evaluator, with equivalent success rates. With CUDA MPS, sixteen workers and four replicas give 6.16× speedup. On RoboTwin Easy, four GPUs with chunk-boundary observation finish 500 episodes in 14.4 minutes, 25.04× faster than the single-GPU baseline, with identical success outcomes and terminal steps. The speedups are measured against the official evaluators and the baselines named in the paper, and the evidence covers two benchmarks in detail. Search time adds 506 s on LIBERO-Long.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: RoboScope Kit wraps models and benchmarks once and separates simulator workers from model replicas to speed evaluation.

digest_headlines.heading: Background and Motivation
digest_headlines.headline: The official StarVLA evaluator leaves the GPU at 14.3% average utilization because simulation and per-step handling dominate CPU time.

digest_headlines.heading: Design
digest_headlines.headline: The design separates simulator workers from Policy replicas and uses a diagonal search to size both from measured probes.

digest_headlines.heading: Implementation
digest_headlines.headline: The implementation packages a Python Policy API, native benchmark evaluators, and a six-family adapter catalog that run as separate local processes.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: RoboScope Kit matches official LIBERO-Long outcomes and evaluates 4.45 times faster than StarVLA, and 6.16 times faster with CUDA MPS.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: The related work places the paper among evaluation harnesses and simulation engines that separate simulators from inference.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Search cost is large on short workloads, so reporting search time beside evaluation time shows when automation pays off.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The system matches official outcomes and cuts evaluation time 4.45 to 6.16 times on LIBERO-Long, and 359.7 to 14.4 minutes on RoboTwin Easy.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists Policy lifecycle methods, benchmark contracts, work-queue states, experimental details, tuning runs, and adapter catalog.

repos.title: Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model
repos.paper_summary: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is a training algorithm that aligns language models with human preferences using a binary cross-entropy loss, eliminating the need for reinforcement learning. DPO derives this objective by reparameterizing the reward function in standard RLHF as $\hat{r}(x,y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)}$, where $\pi_\theta$ is the policy being trained and $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ is a fixed reference model. This substitution allows the optimal policy to be extracted in closed form from the Bradley-Terry preference model. The paper proves that under mild assumptions, this reparameterization preserves the full class of representable reward functions without loss of generality. Experiments on IMDb sentiment generation, Reddit TL;DR summarization, and Anthropic dialogue tasks show DPO matches or exceeds PPO-based RLHF performance. In sentiment control, DPO achieves higher expected reward at equivalent KL-divergence levels than PPO. For summarization and dialogue, GPT-4 evaluations indicate DPO win rates are comparable to or better than PPO baselines. Limitations include evaluation reliance on GPT-4 judgments and untested scaling beyond 6B parameter models.

repos.title: RAG-Anything: All-in-One RAG Framework
repos.paper_summary: RAG-Anything is a unified multimodal retrieval-augmented generation framework that builds a dual graph over documents: a cross-modal graph anchored on non-text units (figures, tables, equations) and a text-based graph, merged by entity-name alignment. Retrieval combines graph neighborhood expansion with dense embedding search over entities, relations, and chunks, and a VLM answers using text context plus the dereferenced visual content. On DocBench, it reaches 63.4% overall accuracy versus 61.0% for MMGraphRAG, 58.4% for LightRAG, and 51.2% for GPT-4o-mini. On MMLongBench, it reaches 42.8% versus 38.9% for LightRAG and 37.7% for MMGraphRAG. The gap grows with document length: on DocBench it is over 13 points for documents over 100 pages. Ablations on DocBench show 60.0% for chunk-only retrieval and 62.4% without the reranker, against 63.4% for the full system. All baselines use GPT-4o-mini, and accuracy is judged by GPT-4o-mini. The paper reports no variance across runs. Evaluation covers two benchmarks only.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing RAG systems handle only text, so multimodal documents are poorly served; the paper proposes RAG-Anything to fix this.

digest_headlines.heading: The RAG-Anything Framework
digest_headlines.headline: RAG-Anything decomposes documents into typed units, builds two linked graphs, and retrieves through both structure and embeddings.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: On MMLongBench, RAG-Anything scores 42.8% overall versus 37.7% for MMGraphRAG, with gains growing on longer documents.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work groups graph-enhanced RAG and multimodal RAG, and argues that prior multimodal systems fragment by modality.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The paper concludes that dual-graph retrieval helps long documents and identifies text-centric bias and rigid spatial processing as failure modes.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists dataset statistics, extra case studies, the three multimodal prompts, the accuracy prompt, and failure-case analyses.

repos.title: RF-DETR: Neural Architecture Search for Real-Time Detection Transformers
repos.paper_summary: RF-DETR is a specialist detection transformer that uses weight-sharing neural architecture search to discover accuracy-latency Pareto curves for target datasets without re-training. The model replaces the LW-DETR backbone with DINOv2 and applies a scheduler-free training procedure. During training, it samples random configurations of image resolution, patch size, windowed attention blocks, decoder layers, and query tokens. At inference, grid search selects specific sub-nets from this single trained model to match hardware constraints. On COCO, RF-DETR (nano) achieves 48.0 AP at 2.3 ms latency, outperforming D-FINE (nano) by 5.3 AP. The 2x-large variant reaches 60.1 AP on COCO, the first real-time detector to exceed 60 AP. On Roboflow100-VL, RF-DETR (2x-large) surpasses GroundingDINO (tiny) by 1.2 AP while running 20 times faster. The paper notes that latency measurements are sensitive to GPU power throttling, proposing a standardized buffering protocol for reproducible benchmarking.

repos.title: Monocular Identity-Conditioned Facial Reflectance Reconstruction
repos.paper_summary: ID2Reflectance is a framework for monocular facial reflectance reconstruction that estimates diffuse albedo, specular albedo, roughness, and surface normal maps from a single in-the-wild image. The method learns a facial prior in image space rather than UV space to reduce dependency on limited light-stage data. It trains a VQGAN with multi-domain codebooks, aligning RGB and reflectance domains by jointly training on FFHQ and 135 captured subjects. An identity-conditioned swapper module, trained on VGGFace2HQ using AdaIN, injects identity features from the target image into the pre-trained decoder. At inference, the system synthesizes three-view reflectance images and stitches them into UV-space maps. On a test set of 20 subjects, ID2Reflectance achieves a PSNR of 28.47 dB for diffuse albedo, outperforming TRUST (21.63 dB) and ID2Albedo (23.72 dB). Identity similarity reaches 0.735 compared to 0.532 for ID2Albedo. The total inference time is 3.8 seconds per face on an A6000 GPU. The paper notes that reconstructed PBR maps may not be physically plausible due to the lack of ground-truth supervision.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Reflectance models trained on few light-stage captures generalize poorly, so the method learns the reflectance prior in image space from abundant RGB faces.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior facial reflectance methods depend on light-stage data and their data is unreleased, while face swapping methods target only the RGB domain.

digest_headlines.heading: Methodology
digest_headlines.headline: Two-stage codebook training aligns reflectance with RGB, so identity swapping learned on RGB transfers to reflectance maps.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Trained on 115 captured subjects, the method gives identity-preserved reflectance on Digital Emily and in-the-wild faces in 3.8 seconds/face.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusions and Discussions
digest_headlines.headline: The paper concludes that limited captured data yields a reliable reflectance prior and notes the method could be misused.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers the light stage rig, public datasets, codebook and swapper details, UV stitching, a fairness benchmark, and further qualitative results.

repos.title: Megatron-LM: Training Multi-Billion Parameter Language Models Using Model Parallelism
repos.paper_summary: The paper presents Megatron-LM, a method for training multi-billion parameter transformer language models using intra-layer model parallelism in PyTorch. The approach partitions the self-attention and MLP blocks across GPUs by splitting weight matrices column-wise for the first linear layer and row-wise for the second, requiring only two all-reduce operations per forward pass. This design avoids custom compilers and is orthogonal to pipeline parallelism. On 512 NVIDIA V100 GPUs, an 8.3 billion parameter GPT-2 model sustains 15.1 PetaFLOPs with 76% scaling efficiency relative to a single-GPU baseline. The same architecture trains a 3.9 billion parameter BERT variant, where rearranging layer normalization before residual connections prevents degradation observed in standard BERT at larger scales. The 8.3B GPT-2 model achieves a WikiText103 perplexity of 10.8 and LAMBADA accuracy of 66.5%, while the 3.9B BERT model reaches 90.9% accuracy on RACE. Limitations include the requirement for high-bandwidth interconnects like NVLink or InfiniBand, and the fact that the BERT results are reported on development sets for most tasks except RACE.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Megatron-LM trains transformers up to 8.3 billion parameters with intra-layer model parallelism, reaching 76% scaling efficiency on 512 GPUs.

digest_headlines.heading: Background and Challenges
digest_headlines.headline: Existing model parallel methods need custom compilers or pipeline changes, so the authors modify only a PyTorch transformer.

digest_headlines.heading: Model Parallel Transformers
digest_headlines.headline: The MLP and attention blocks are split across GPUs so each transformer layer needs only four all-reduce operations.

digest_headlines.heading: Setup
digest_headlines.headline: GPT-2 and BERT models train on an aggregated 174 GB deduplicated corpus with fixed optimizer and learning-rate schedules.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Model parallel scaling reaches 77% of linear scaling at 8.3 billion parameters, and GPT-2 and BERT results set new SOTA marks.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion and Future Work
digest_headlines.headline: The authors conclude that intra-layer parallelism scales to 8.3 billion parameters and suggest hybrid parallelism for larger models.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists BERT finetuning hyperparameters, hybrid parallelism and random number details, text samples, evaluation methodology, and strong scaling results.

repos.title: CoworkOS:Scaling Agent Coworkers for Real-world Automation
repos.paper_summary: CoworkOS is an agent harness for long-horizon human-agent work. Its three layers are a Main Agent that chooses actions, delegations, and acceptance; a Coordinator Runtime that routes messages and tracks state; and optional Subagents that run in isolated contexts, synchronously or asynchronously. Humans and agents edit the same versioned resources (documents, presentations, CAD models, Blender scenes). A commit rule checks each edit's base revision and returns a conflict for stale edits. Persistent workspaces, semantic memory, and background Jobs with logs let work resume after interruption. The paper reports competitiveness with OpenHands, Codex, and DeepSeek Harness across 12 benchmarks and six application categories, but the text gives no per-benchmark scores for these comparisons. In a post-training case study, CoworkOS ran five rounds on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and the average over eight benchmarks rose from 33.19 to 42.95 (+9.76). Limitations: the study covers one model, the authors state that gains vary across tasks, and the benchmark count is 12 in the abstract but 10 in one figure caption.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: CoworkOS splits task strategy from execution so one agent can handle complex delivery and long-horizon monitoring.

digest_headlines.heading: Preliminaries: Task Formulation and Agency
digest_headlines.headline: Agent tasks are defined by objective, environment, actions, acceptance, and budget, judged along complexity and temporal extent.

digest_headlines.heading: The CoworkOS Agent Harness
digest_headlines.headline: A three-layer harness with synchronous or asynchronous delegation, shared application objects, and durable workspaces and memory.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: CoworkOS ranks among the top two harnesses in every domain average, leading Productivity and ML Coding.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Post-training gains vary across tasks, and the paper concludes that one harness supports productivity, monitoring, and model improvement.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix lists benchmark settings, scoring rules, case inspection protocols, and post-training run records with complete round scores.
